text: Track 4.1 Welcome everyone. My name's Marianne. The topic of my presentation today is conservation development in the UK. Okay, so my presentation is going to be in four parts. First, I'm going to briefly explain what conservation development is, as some of you may not know. Next, I'm going to explain the impact of humans on natural habitats. Then, I'll outline some of the work that conservation organisations do to protect bird habitats. And finally, I shall be suggesting how we can, as individuals, help to protect wildlife by thinking a little more about conservation and making small changes in our gardens. Okay, so let's begin with a brief explanation of what conservation development is. It combines social development, that is, the need to develop land for farming or to build new homes, with protecting the environment and the habitat of wildlife species. A conservation development project is usually managed and controlled by the owner of the land, for example, an individual, a business, the local government, or a conservation organisation like the RSPB, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds. By combining conservation with development, communities can still access the resources they require, but in a way which does not create a harsh environmental impact. Okay, so now I want to move on to my next point and tell you how natural habitats have been affected. As I mentioned before, the way we farm our land can affect natural habitats. This is particularly the case for farmland birds. Many farmland bird species are small seed-eating birds. As a direct result of changes in farming methods and crops grown, bird numbers have declined overall by over 9% since 1980, and some species have declined by as much as 70%. Let me tell you why. There has been an increase in farming crops like corn and a reduction of farming vegetables like turnips and carrots. These birds depend on eating seeds from the small plants that were allowed to grow naturally among the vegetable crops. Now the vegetable crops have been replaced, the plants which the birds relied on for food have almost disappeared. Because seed-eating birds cannot easily adapt to eating other foods, they have found it particularly difficult to survive in winter when conditions are harsh. So how have RSPB's projects been successful? Well, they have educated farmers by providing advice about what crops can be introduced to support farmland birds' natural habitat. Where it is not possible to completely change the crop, they have suggested small areas of land are left to go wild. That is not farmed and left for nature to control. Typically, this might be a metre or two around the edge of a field that is, say, used to grow corn. Local government has also supported these projects by providing conservation advice. In addition, farmers who have lost income by changing their farming methods to help protect wildlife can receive financial support. Okay, so you might be thinking that we, as individuals, cannot do much to help wildlife conservation. But this is not the case, which brings me to my final point. How can we help? Well, if you are lucky enough to have a garden, you can provide birds with fresh drinking water. This might be a simple bird bath or a small pond which could be used by other water-loving creatures, like frogs. You could have a wildlife garden. For example, you could grow plants and flowers which attract bees and other flying insects. In winter, you can feed birds with seeds. But remember, if you start doing this and attract more birds into your garden, you should keep doing it or they might die. Right, well, we're out of time now, but please come and see me later if you would like more information about how you can get involved in wildlife conservation.
